title: Place Transition Words by Logic
description: Use transition-word punctuation and three-clause logic to decide whether a transition belongs before or after a full stop in SAT Boundaries questions.

blocks.html:
Where does the transition belong?

Some SAT Boundaries questions give you two choices that are both grammatically possible:

  • a transition just before a semicolon or period
  • the same transition just after that semicolon or period

Punctuation alone will not separate those choices. You must decide which two ideas the transition connects.

By the end of this lesson, you will be able to attach a transition to the correct independent clause and use the logic among three clauses to place it.

Compare two placements

Read these versions:

Version 1: The first soil sample contained pollen. The second sample, however, contained no pollen.

Version 2: The first soil sample contained pollen. The second sample contained no pollen, however.

The word however moves, but the relationship it expresses does not. In both versions, notice which two facts contrast.

content.prompt: In both sample sentences, which two ideas does however contrast?
choices: pollen and soil
the second sample and the word pollen
the first sample contained pollen and the second sample contained no pollen
the placement of the first period and the placement of the second period
content.hint: Temporarily move however to the beginning of the second sentence: 'However, the second sample contained no pollen.'
content.explanation: Correct. However marks a contrast between the complete idea before it and the complete idea in the clause that contains it. Moving the word within the second clause does not change that relationship.

blocks.html:
A transition shows the relationship between ideas

A transition word or phrase tells you how the current independent clause relates to the previous independent clause.

  • however, nevertheless, though: contrast
  • therefore, consequently, thus: cause and result
  • moreover, furthermore, in addition: addition
  • for example, specifically: example or detail

An independent clause is a complete sentence: it has a subject, a verb, and a finished thought.

Key idea: The transition belongs to one independent clause and points backward to the independent clause before it.

content.prompt: What is the main job of however in this passage? The first trial succeeded. The second trial, however, failed.
choices: It shows that the second trial contrasts with the first trial.
It turns the second trial into a question.
It makes the first clause dependent on the second.
It replaces the verb in the second clause.
content.hint: Read the two results: succeeded and failed. What relationship do they have?
content.explanation: Right. However tells you that the current clause's failure contrasts with the previous clause's success.

blocks.html:
The transition is nonessential information

A transition adds a logical signpost, but it is not needed to make the clause complete. Remove however below:

The second trial, however, failed.

You are left with The second trial failed, which is still a complete sentence. Because the transition is nonessential, punctuation separates it from the essential words of its clause.

  • Beginning: However, the second trial failed.
  • Middle: The second trial, however, failed.
  • End: The second trial failed, however.

At a clause boundary, a period or semicolon can close the clause where a second comma might otherwise appear: The second trial failed, however; the team repeated it.

content.prompt: Which test shows that nevertheless is nonessential in this sentence? The sensor, nevertheless, recorded the change.
choices: Move the sensor to the end of the sentence.
Replace recorded with a different verb.
Add a second subject after nevertheless.
Remove nevertheless and its commas; 'The sensor recorded the change' remains complete.
content.hint: Nonessential information can be removed without destroying the sentence's grammatical core.
content.explanation: Exactly. Removing the transition leaves a complete independent clause, so the transition is nonessential and must be offset by punctuation.

blocks.html:
A transition can appear anywhere in its clause

At the beginning, in the middle, and at the very end are all possible. The placement changes emphasis, not the direction of the connection.

  • However, the backup system worked.
  • The backup system, however, worked.
  • The backup system worked, however.

Watch out: A sentence absolutely can end with a transition word or phrase.

In every version, however belongs to the clause about the backup system and points backward to the independent clause before it.

One transition is pickier: though cannot lead its clause. You will practice that special case later in this lesson.

content.prompt: Which statement about transition placement is accurate?
choices: A transition must begin its independent clause.
A transition may begin, interrupt, or end its independent clause.
A transition at the end points forward to the next clause.
A transition becomes essential when it appears in the middle.
content.hint: Recall the three grammatical versions of 'the backup system worked.'
content.explanation: Correct. A transition can occur anywhere in its clause, including at the very end.

blocks.html:
Even at the end, the transition points backward

Read this pair:

The forecast predicted clear skies. A storm arrived, however.

However does not point ahead to an unwritten idea. It belongs to A storm arrived and connects that current clause backward to The forecast predicted clear skies.

To find the logic, ask: What complete clause contains the transition, and what complete clause comes immediately before it?

content.prompt: In 'The forecast predicted clear skies. A storm arrived, however,' what does however connect?
choices: It connects storm to an idea that must appear in the next sentence.
It connects clear to skies inside the first clause.
It connects 'A storm arrived' backward to 'The forecast predicted clear skies.'
It connects only the subjects forecast and storm.
content.hint: Identify the complete clause that contains however, then look one independent clause backward.
content.explanation: Right. Sentence-final however still belongs to the storm clause and points backward to the forecast clause.

blocks.html:
The SAT trap uses three independent clauses

Now suppose a passage contains three complete ideas. Label them A, B, and C.

The choices may include both of these:

  • B, however; C
  • B; however, C

Both can be grammatically correct. The semicolon is a full stop between B and C. The commas show which clause contains the nonessential transition.

  • In B, however; C, however is at the end of B. It connects A to B.
  • In B; however, C, however is at the beginning of C. It connects B to C.

Attach first; judge the logic second

Transition before the full stop: A → transition B | C

Transition after the full stop: A | B → transition C

When the transition belongs to B, test the relationship between A and B. When it belongs to C, test the relationship between B and C.

A period works the same way as a semicolon here. The key question is not which full stop looks stronger. It is which pair of clauses has the relationship named by the transition.

content.prompt: If a choice creates 'A. B, therefore; C,' which relationship must therefore describe?
choices: C must be a result of A.
B must be a result of A.
C must be a result of B.
A must be a result of C.
content.hint: Therefore appears before the semicolon, at the end of B. Move it to the beginning of B.
content.explanation: Correct. Read it mentally as 'A. Therefore, B. C.' Therefore belongs to B and marks B as a result of A.

blocks.html:
Use the A–B–C process

  1. Label: Find the three independent clauses and call them A, B, and C.
  2. Attach: Use the punctuation to decide whether the transition belongs to B or C.
  3. Move: If the transition is at the end of a clause, mentally move it to the beginning of that same clause.
  4. Test: Read one clause backward and check whether the transition's meaning fits that pair.

Decision rule: Before the full stop means test A–B. After the full stop means test B–C.

Model: the transition belongs to B

Read all three clauses:

A: The observatory's main telescope was under repair. B: Astronomers used a smaller backup telescope ___ C: The backup instrument had been installed in 2018.

The two serious choices are , therefore; and ; therefore,.

First test the logic. The repair caused the astronomers to use a backup, so A leads to B. Using the backup did not cause it to be installed in 2018, so B does not lead to C.

content.prompt: Where must therefore go in the observatory passage?
choices: After the semicolon, because C is a result of B
After the semicolon, because A is a result of C
Before the semicolon, because C is a result of A
Before the semicolon, because B is a result of A
content.hint: Ask which event is the result of the telescope being under repair.
content.explanation: Exactly. B is a result of A, so therefore belongs to B and must appear before the full stop between B and C.

blocks.html:
Complete the model

The correct punctuation is:

The observatory's main telescope was under repair. Astronomers used a smaller backup telescope, therefore; the backup instrument had been installed in 2018.

Mental rewrite: The observatory's main telescope was under repair. Therefore, astronomers used a smaller backup telescope. The backup instrument had been installed in 2018.

The original sentence-final placement is less familiar, but it expresses the same A-to-B logic.

content.prompt: The museum's climate-control system failed. Staff moved the paintings to a protected storage room ___ the room was renovated in 2022. Which choice fits the logic?
choices: , consequently;
; consequently,
, consequently,
; consequently;
content.solution:
Label the clauses: A is "The museum's climate-control system failed," B is "Staff moved the paintings to a protected storage room," and C is "the room was renovated in 2022."
Test the logic to find the result pair: the system failure caused the move, so B is a result of A; moving the paintings did not cause the 2022 renovation, so C is not a result of B.
Attach: consequently connects A to B, so it belongs at the end of B, before the full stop, which is ", consequently;". Placing it after the semicolon would attach it to C and wrongly test B to C.
Verify with the mental rewrite: "The museum's climate-control system failed. Consequently, staff moved the paintings to a protected storage room. The room was renovated in 2022."
So the answer is choice A, ", consequently;".
content.hint: Label the clauses A, B, and C. The system failure caused which clause: B or C?
content.explanation: Correct. A caused B, so consequently belongs at the end of B, before the semicolon. Moving it gives: 'The system failed. Consequently, staff moved the paintings.'

blocks.html:
Now the transition belongs to C

Read a new set of clauses:

A: Repairs to the telescope ended on Monday. B: Astronomers expected to resume observations that night ___ C: Dense clouds covered the sky.

A naturally leads to B: finished repairs explain the expectation. The contrast occurs between B and C: the astronomers expected to observe, but clouds blocked the sky.

Therefore, however must belong to C and appear after the full stop between B and C.

content.prompt: Repairs to the telescope ended on Monday. Astronomers expected to resume observations that night ___ dense clouds covered the sky. Which choice fits the logic?
choices: , however;
, however,
; however,
; however;
content.solution:
Label the clauses: A is "Repairs to the telescope ended on Monday," B is "Astronomers expected to resume observations that night," and C is "dense clouds covered the sky."
Test the logic: A leads naturally to B, since finished repairs explain the expectation, so there is no contrast between A and B; the contrast is between B and C, because the astronomers expected to observe but clouds blocked the sky.
Attach: however connects B to C, so it belongs at the beginning of C, after the full stop; the semicolon ends B and "however," begins C.
Verify: "Astronomers expected to resume observations that night; however, dense clouds covered the sky" states the contrast between the right pair.
So the answer is choice C, "; however,".
content.hint: The contrast is between the expectation in B and the clouds in C. Attach however to the clause about the clouds.
content.explanation: Right. The semicolon ends B, and 'however,' begins C. The transition points backward from C to the contrasting expectation in B.

blocks.html:
A period creates the same placement decision

These semicolon patterns have period twins:

  • B, however; C has the same attachment as B, however. C. However belongs to B.
  • B; however, C has the same attachment as B. However, C. However belongs to C.

A semicolon and a period are both full stops. When both answers are grammatically complete, use A–B–C logic to decide which side owns the transition.

content.prompt: The archive lost power. Staff carried the manuscripts to a secure room ___ room had opened five years earlier. Which period choice expresses the correct cause-and-result relationship?
choices: . Consequently, the
, consequently. The
, consequently, the
; consequently; the
content.hint: The power loss caused staff to carry the manuscripts. It did not cause the room to open years earlier. Put consequently in B, before the period.
content.explanation: Correct. Consequently belongs to B because B results from A: 'The archive lost power. Consequently, staff carried the manuscripts.' The transition can sit at the end of B before the period.

blocks.html:
Move a sentence-final transition in your mind

A transition at the end can feel strange because students see beginning transitions more often. Do not reject it. Move it to the beginning of the same clause.

  • Original: A. B, therefore; C.
  • Mental rewrite: A. Therefore, B. C.

Do not move it across the full stop into C. The rewrite is only a thinking tool that makes the backward connection easier to hear.

Tip: Keep the transition inside its original clause when you move it.

content.prompt: Which mental rewrite correctly clarifies 'A. B, nevertheless; C'?
choices: Nevertheless, A. B. C.
A. B. Nevertheless, C.
A. B; C, nevertheless.
A. Nevertheless, B. C.
content.hint: Nevertheless appears inside B before the full stop. Move it to the beginning of B, not into A or C.
content.explanation: Exactly. The mental rewrite keeps nevertheless in B: 'A. Nevertheless, B. C.' Now it is easier to test the A–B contrast.

blocks.html:
Watch for the special word though

Though can do two different jobs.

  • Transition: The forecast predicted rain. The match continued, though.
  • Subordinating word: Though the forecast predicted rain ...

In the first version, though means however. It is nonessential and separated by a comma.

In the second version, though is followed directly by a subject and verb, with no comma after though. It makes the idea dependent: Though the forecast predicted rain cannot stand alone.

Position tells you the job: as a transition meaning however, though appears only in the middle or at the end of its clause. At the front of a clause, though is always the subordinating word.

content.prompt: In which choice does though act as a nonessential transition meaning however?
choices: The match continued, though.
Though the match continued.
Though the match continued, the rain intensified.
The match that continued though the rain.
content.hint: Look for a complete independent clause that remains complete when though is removed.
content.explanation: Correct. Remove ', though' and 'The match continued' remains complete. Here though is a nonessential transition pointing backward.

blocks.html:
Two fast rules for though at the front of a clause

Because the transition job belongs only to the middle and end of a clause, an answer choice that puts though first can be judged immediately:

  • Initial though + comma (. Though, or ; though,) — the choice is treating though like However, — a position though cannot take. Eliminate it on sight.
  • Initial though + no comma (though the crews kept working) — though is the subordinating word, so the clause is dependent. It is correct only when a main clause follows in the same sentence. Standing alone after a period, it is a fragment; after a semicolon, it breaks the independent-clause rule.

Contrast with however: However, the field remained wet is fine. Though, the field remained wet is not. The two words share a meaning — not a position.

choices: The forecast called for rain. Though, the crews kept working.
The forecast called for rain; though the crews kept working.
The forecast called for rain. The crews, though, kept working.
The forecast called for rain. Though the crews kept working.
content.hint: As a transition, though never leads its clause. When though is first, it is the subordinating word — then check what that does to the sentence.
content.explanation: Correct. Mid-clause with commas, though is a valid transition. The first version treats though like However, — a position it cannot take. The second puts a dependent clause after a semicolon, and the fourth leaves a dependent clause standing alone as a fragment.

blocks.html:
No comma can reveal a dependent-clause trap

Compare these fragments after a semicolon:

  • ; the field, though, remained wet — the commas set though off as an inserted transition meaning however, so the field remained wet is independent.
  • ; though the field remained wet — though sits at the front of the clause with no comma after it, so though the field remained wet is dependent.

A semicolon must have an independent clause on both sides. Therefore, a choice that creates ; though + subject + verb with no comma after though can be eliminated: the words after the semicolon are not an independent clause.

Watch out: With though, check its position and its commas before deciding which job the word performs.

content.prompt: Why is the punctuation invalid in 'The organizers kept the outdoor venue; though the field remained wet'?
choices: A semicolon can never appear near the word though.
The clause before the semicolon is missing a verb.
Without a comma after though, 'though the field remained wet' is dependent, so it cannot stand after a semicolon.
The word though always points forward to the next sentence.
content.hint: Read only the words after the semicolon. Can 'Though the field remained wet' stand alone?
content.explanation: Right. Here though is a subordinating word, not a nonessential transition. It creates a dependent clause after a punctuation mark that requires an independent clause.

blocks.html:
Put the whole process together

For each final question:

  1. Label A, B, and C.
  2. Decide which pair has the named relationship.
  3. Attach the transition to B or C.
  4. Use the commas and full stop to select the choice.

Remember to read one independent clause earlier than the blank. Without A, you cannot tell whether a transition at the end of B makes sense.

content.prompt: The river flooded the lower trail. Park officials closed that route ___ the upper trail remained open throughout the week. Which choice best fits the logic?
choices: ; consequently,
, consequently;
, consequently,
; consequently;
content.hint: The flood in A caused the closure in B. The closure did not cause the upper trail to remain open. Attach consequently to B.
content.explanation: Correct. Consequently belongs to B because B results from A: 'The river flooded the lower trail. Consequently, park officials closed that route.' The sentence-final transition comes before the semicolon.

content.prompt: The new battery passed every laboratory test. Engineers expected it to last ten hours in the field ___ it stopped working after only six hours. Which choice best fits the logic?
choices: , however;
, however,
; however;
; however,
content.hint: The contrast is between the ten-hour expectation in B and the six-hour result in C. Attach however to C.
content.explanation: Exactly. However begins C after the semicolon and points backward to the contrasting expectation in B.

content.prompt: Without looking back, which process solves the transition-placement question type?
choices: Label A–B–C; attach the transition to B or C; move an end transition within its clause if helpful; test A–B or B–C logic; check whether though is truly a transition.
Label A–B–C; attach the transition to A or B; move an end transition into the next clause; test A–C logic; check whether though is truly a transition.
Label A–B–C; test A–B or B–C logic before attaching the transition; leave an end transition where it stands; treat though as a transition whenever it starts a clause.
Attach the transition to whichever clause is longest; label A–B–C afterward to confirm; test both A–B and B–C and keep whichever choice fits either.
content.hint: Retrieve the labels, attachment rule, movement trick, logic pair, and though check.
content.explanation: You have it. Before the full stop means test A–B; after the full stop means test B–C. A transition may end its clause, and though without the transition comma may create a dependent clause instead.

content.html:
You can place transitions by logic

You can identify the clause that owns a transition, trace its backward connection, compare A–B with B–C, and handle sentence-final transitions and the special though trap.
